summary:
Rwanda does not criminalise same-sex intimacy. The age of consent is 18 regardless of sexual orientation or gender, and no statute criminalises transgender identity or consensual relationships as such.

Rwandan law forbids changing legal gender, so no legal gender recognition path exists. A trans visitor's documents cannot be aligned with their lived gender under local law, and identity checks are where that absence becomes an enforcement encounter. The Human Rights First Rwanda Association's 2025 submission to the UN Human Rights Committee documents law-enforcement abuse directed at transgender people: harassment during identity checks and arbitrary arrests on vagrancy and public-order grounds.

Violent detentions of transgender people were reported by Vice on 20 November 2020. On Christmas Day 2018, Bella, a singer booked to perform at a hotel in Kigali, was stopped by police officers on the street after her show; her name was changed over concerns for her safety. The most recent documented incident in this record is the 2025 submission to the UN Human Rights Committee; no later individual case is documented.

A 2016 report by the U.S. State Department recorded that LGBTQ Rwandans had been harassed, blackmailed and arrested by police under public-order and morality laws, and that LGBTI rights groups reported harassment by neighbours and police. That figure dates the reporting window to 2016, and no prevalence figure covering a later period appears in these sources.

The Constitution, adopted in May 2003, provides in Article 26 that only civil monogamous marriage between a man and a woman is recognised; same-sex marriages, civil unions and equivalent arrangements are not recognised. A trans visitor in a relationship that would be classed locally as same-sex therefore has no recognition route in Rwanda.

No anti-discrimination law protects LGBTQ people. The Constitution's non-discrimination provisions, Articles 15 and 16, do not list sexual orientation or gender identity as protected grounds. Three limited instruments do reach sexual orientation: the Human Resource Management Policy (2015) of the Office of the Auditor General of State Finances lists sexual orientation as a prohibited ground for harassment, the Code of Conduct of the Public Private Partnership Guidelines (2018) bans discrimination against bidders on that ground, and Law 058/2021 on Protection of Personal Data and Privacy treats a person's sexual life as sensitive personal data.

Health services carry an explicit equal-access guarantee: the Patients Rights and Responsibilities Policy (2018) of the Ministry of Health states that all Rwandans, regardless of gender, sexual orientation, age, religion, cultural belief or disability, are equally entitled to receive health services, and the policy applies across the public, private and NGO sectors.

Protection machinery for people seeking international protection names gender identity directly. The government issued immigration and asylum protections covering LGBTQ people in 2024, and in April 2022 a transgender claimant was granted refugee status. The Asylum and humanitarian protection decision-making Standard Operating Procedures (2024) require that interviews be conducted so the individual can present the grounds of the application comprehensively, with trained interviewers taking account of gender and any circumstance including sexual orientation, gender identity or vulnerability. The Manual on Refugee Appeal Tribunal Standard Operating Procedures (2014) requires hearings to take account of the appellant's sexual orientation, gender identity or vulnerability, and the Standard Operating Procedures on identifying and safeguarding vulnerable persons under the Migration and Economic Development Partnership (2024) define Vulnerable Persons to include individuals whose gender identity or sexual orientation places them at higher risk, expressly naming lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons.

Organisation itself is constrained. LGBTIQ organisations cannot register openly, and NGO Law No. 058/2024, adopted in June 2024, raises freedom-of-association concerns. A public Pride event was held in 2021.
tangentialFactors:
Official posture has been stated as non-engagement rather than protection. President Paul Kagame told an audience at Rwanda Cultural Day in San Francisco on 25 September 2016 that homosexuality "hasn't been our problem. And we don't intend to make it our problem." The same year, a public assertion of gay identity drew a reaction that the sources treat as exceptional: in September 2019 gospel singer Albert Nabonibo came out on a Christian YouTube channel, drawing shock and hostile reactions from family and friends, while the Minister of State for East African Community Affairs, Olivier Nduhungirehe, publicly backed him.

The sources available here contain no trans-specific violence count with a denominator, and no figure comparing transgender victimisation to Rwanda's general homicide rate. No such comparison can be stated from this inventory, and none is offered.

Social climate is described by the sources as one in which homosexuality is a taboo subject with little public discussion and LGBTQ people face stigmatisation among the broader population. Institutional voices have included opposition: the Anglican Church of Rwanda condemned what it called non-biblical behaviour by Western churches in 2007 and refused to support ordination of LGBTQ clergy.
localsOnly:
The Horizons Community Association of Rwanda has conducted public advocacy for LGBTQ rights since 2005, and its members have often been harassed by the government.

Open registration is not available to LGBTIQ organisations, and NGO Law No. 058/2024, adopted June 2024, adds association constraints that bear directly on residents organising collectively.

For residents, the practical protections are narrow and sector-specific: sexual orientation appears as a prohibited ground for harassment in the Office of the Auditor General of State Finances Human Resource Management Policy (2015) and as a banned ground for discriminating against bidders under the Public Private Partnership Guidelines Code of Conduct (2018), while Law 058/2021 on Protection of Personal Data and Privacy classifies sexual life as sensitive personal data. Constitutional Articles 15 and 16 supply no sexual-orientation or gender-identity protection, and there is no general LGBTQ anti-discrimination statute.

The Ministry of Health's Patients Rights and Responsibilities Policy (2018) binds public, private and NGO providers to treat all Rwandans equally regardless of gender and sexual orientation, which is the strongest formal guarantee of care access on the books.
outOfScopeNotes:
No trans-specific violence or killing statistic for Rwanda appears in this inventory, so no figure, rate or ranking can be given; the absence of a number is not evidence of an absence of harm.

The inventory contains no findings on border or airport document screening, gender markers on passports, or how Rwandan authorities treat identity documents issued abroad in a gender the traveller now lives in. That gap is unresolved here, not settled either way.

How Rwandan authorities would classify the marriage or partnership of a trans person whose documents were issued abroad, and whether Article 26's man-woman formulation would be applied on birth-sex status, is not sourced and remains unresolved.

No youth-, minor- or education-specific findings appear in the sources: no school policy, no documentation on bullying, and no guidance on minors' access to gender-affirming medication or on carrying such medication.

The most recent individual incident documented here is from 2018, with violent-detention reporting in November 2020 and a documented pattern of identity-check abuse in a 2025 submission to a UN treaty body; no later individual case is recorded, and no prevalence figure covering a defined recent period exists in these sources.
